title: More than 43 million ballots cast so far in midterms early voting surge
description: With less than a week to go until the US midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress for the next two years, more than 43 mi
body: With less than a week to go until the US midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress for the next two years, more than 43 million Americans have already voted.Data from the University of Florida Election Lab indicates that four to five million early votes have been cast each day, representing a much higher rate than in most previous elections. Texas has seen the highest above-average turnout rate so far, says Prof Mike McDonald, who runs the Election Lab database. Hispanic communities are also seeing a much higher turnout than usual. Overall turnout appears on track to outpace 2020, or even 2018, which beat the 1914 record for overall turnout in a midterm election.Texas has already surpassed its 2022 numbers by around 1.75 million voters, says McDonald. More than 5.8 million ballots have already been cast in the Lone Star state, which has emerged as a key battleground that could decide which party controls the Senate for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. Data from states that require voters to register a political affiliation indicates an increase is votes cast by Democrats, while Republican early voting numbers remain generally similar to 2022.Early voting is also up among voters who chose to not register with a specific party, McDonald says, however the data does not show which candidates they chose. Figures on Thursday, external show that 44% of early ballots have been cast by Democrats, and 31.2% by Republicans. A further 24.7% were attributed to voters who had no party affiliation. However, that's just for the roughly half of states that require voter affiliation.Three states require voters to submit their race when they register - North Carolina, Georgia and Florida. Data from these states shows an increase in votes cast by Hispanic and black communities, while voting among white people is on par with 2022 early voting figures. "That makes sense because communities of colour are more frequently part of the Democratic coalition, and whites are more frequently part of the Republican coalition," McDonald says.Texas does not require voters to provide party affiliation or race. But the data still shows a surge in voting by some counties on the border with Mexico, which are comprised of more than 90% Hispanic people."When I look at those counties, what I see is some of them are going to beat their 2022 turnout in just the early vote alone," says McDonald.Early voting has boomed in recent years, driven by the Covid pandemic when more states began offering early voting options, including both in-person and by mail. In the 2020 election, when voters were picking both the next president as well as their lawmakers, more than two-thirds of all ballots were cast early. Half of those early votes were also cast by mail. Voters increasingly prefer to vote in-person, even when voting early, says McDonald. They are also returning their ballots earlier than in previous elections. He adds that he believes this could be due to concerns about postal voting, but says there is not data to indicate what could be causing this. Postal votes are more likely to be disqualified due to errors, he notes, and says some voters could be concerned about meddling in the US Postal Service. Some officials have already confirmed records being broken. On Thursday, the city of Minneapolis said that it has set an early voting record for a non-presidential election.Early voting will soon taper off, as states start cutting off early voting as an option in the days before the election on Tuesday, 3 November.

schema.headline: More than 43 million ballots cast so far in midterms early voting surge

title: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
description: It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls sho
body: It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model. A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power. While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected. There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge. Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030. The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.

schema.headline: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate

title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
description: Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in We
body: Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold. However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, external, Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.The change applies to payments made from 28 October.In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner". Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system. "Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

schema.headline: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules

title: Paris suburb shooting suspect targeted people of Muslim or African appearance, prosecutor says
description: A man suspected of a deadly shooting near Paris last week has admitted targeting people of "Muslim, African or North African" appearance, prosecutors
body: A man suspected of a deadly shooting near Paris last week has admitted targeting people of "Muslim, African or North African" appearance, prosecutors say.A man was killed and seven people including a child were injured last Friday when an attacker opened fire as he drove through two western suburbs.On Thursday the suspect was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office (PNAT) said.President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack" and anti-racism demonstrations have been held around France.Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was killed in the shooting. Three of those wounded were still in hospital with one in critical condition, terrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen told reporters.The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, chose Trappes and nearby La Verrière because he saw them as a "hotbed for Islamists", he said.Kevin T had denied any "terrorist intent",  insisted his actions were "legitimate" and said he "feels no regret", Christen said.Police found "weapons or weapon components" in the suspect's home as well as books including a Quran, a Bible and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf and stickers celebrating the hard-right National Rally (RN) party, Christen said.Kevin T told investigators that he had designed the stickers with slogans such as "long live France, RN, proud to be French" himself and had them printed more than a year ago, Christen said.But the suspect also told investigators he was not a member or supporter of any political party.On Wednesday Macron said that "certain political movements on the far right" including the RN and "those close to them" had allowed a climate of racism "to take root".Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a prominent RN lawmaker, retorted that it was the president himself who had allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish.France's presidential elections is six months away and RN leader Marine Le Pen is currently leading opinion polls.

schema.headline: Paris suburb shooting suspect targeted people of Muslim or African appearance, prosecutor says

title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan letter
description: The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, wh
body: The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".Confirming that it had referred itself to the IOPC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter. "While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said. It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC. The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings."If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble."I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'. Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received". "If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said. "I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."Reports of the Met's handline of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

schema.headline: Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan letter

title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
description: Warning: This story contains graphic content.Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our ch
body: Warning: This story contains graphic content.Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."Laura Brand is the daughter of former golfer Bernard Gallacher and sister of TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher. She married Brand in 2017 and they have three children.She told the court she first met him at the Edinburgh festival in 2006, explaining that he took her number and they started a relationship soon afterwards.She said that after his performance: "I went over and said, 'I'm Laura, Kirsty's sister. That was a great show'."He contacted her the next day, she said. When they met, she said they had oral sex, adding: "He might have wanted to have sex but I didn't want to."Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others."I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said."I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage."It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriendsElia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with"."When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her."He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'

title: MI5 false evidence in neo-Nazi spy case a serious failure, says intelligence watchdog
description: The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of the UK's intelligence services has said that MI5 lying to multiple courts while defending a violent
body: The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of the UK's intelligence services has said that MI5 lying to multiple courts while defending a violent neo-Nazi spy is as "serious as anything" he has ever dealt with."Oversight depends on candour," said investigatory powers commissioner Lord Leveson. "Failings of candour undermine the entire basis of oversight and accountability."His office, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office (IPCO), investigated how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts concerning the abusive informant known as agent X, as first exposed by the BBC. IPCO's report, released earlier this year, found one senior officer lied repeatedly while another misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.It also criticised other senior spies and found "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.MI5 said it accepted the report's findings "without reservation" last month. The High Court is due to decide soon on what action, if any, to take against the agency or its staff.In comments to mark the publication of his annual report on Thursday, Lord Leveson said the "case of agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as commissioner"."False evidence was given to the High Court and the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and the prime minister directed me to find out how that happened."My investigation has now concluded and found that both IPCO and the courts were misled."The IPCO investigation examined how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the violent neo-Nazi informant.He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while he was under police investigation.The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block our investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.MI5 claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from Beth and everyone else, leaving her at a serious disadvantage.But what MI5 said was untrue. It had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.A senior MI5 officer had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. He even wanted me to meet the agent. In doing so, he repeatedly departed from the NCND policy.That officer was found to have repeatedly lied by the IPCO investigation. He has resigned from MI5 since the BBC exposed what happened.The IPCO also oversees and regulates MI6 and GCHQ, as well covert powers and agent-running by police forces and other agencies.Its annual report revealed that errors by MI5 involving agents increased from four in 2017 to 21 in 2025. In the same period, errors by MI6 decreased from 10 to three.It also criticised the National Crime Agency (NCA) for failings in how it managed a juvenile criminal informant, meaning a child under 18 who was being used by the agency.It found that the NCA did not inform Lord Leveson of the fact it was running a child informant within the required time period, and a senior NCA officer wrongly extended the authorisation well beyond what is legal. It also found a failure to record the circumstances which would justify the absence of an "appropriate adult", and that the child was "tasked to engage in criminal conduct" without the protection of a valid legal authorisation.Lord Leveson said the agency's conduct fell "well short of what the law requires" and said he had written to its director general.He also expressed concern with GCHQ, saying it "still cannot tell me what has happened to removable media that may hold sensitive data, years after I first raised it with them".The report revealed the spy agency now estimates there are "thousands" of memory cards, hard drives and other portable media items it can neither find nor account for. The report stated that "these items are utilised extensively and are an essential component of some of GCHQ's operating processes"."We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate", said Lord Leveson.

schema.headline: MI5 false evidence in neo-Nazi spy case a serious failure, says intelligence watchdog

title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
description: The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare
body: The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones."Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed.""I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said."People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week."They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said."This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive." On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable."Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground. "An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon. But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.But the clock is ticking. The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said. "We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months."These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

schema.headline: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next

title: Jack Grealish: England winger dropped by Everton due to 'breach of club discipline'
description: Jack Grealish was left out of Everton's Carabao Cup tie with Newcastle United on Thursday  "due to a breach of club discipline"., externalEverton did
body: Jack Grealish was left out of Everton's Carabao Cup tie with Newcastle United on Thursday  "due to a breach of club discipline"., externalEverton did not disclose any further details but it is understood to arise from an unauthorised absence from training.Everton overcame Grealish's absence to win 3-1 and book a quarter-final tie at League Two Fleetwood Town.England winger Grealish, 31, is on loan at Everton from Premier League rivals Manchester City.He spent a large chunk of last season with the Toffees under a similar arrangement, scoring twice and providing six assists in 20 appearances, before sustaining a season-ending foot injury in January.Grealish came on as a substitute during City's 3-0 Community Shield defeat to Arsenal at Wembley in August.The former Aston Villa player, who cost City £100m in 2021, also featured as a substitute during City's 2-1 win over Bournemouth on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.He returned to Everton before the transfer window closed and has featured five times for them this season in the Premier League.Grealish also played in Everton's Carabao Cup third round win over Wolves.

schema.headline: Jack Grealish: England winger dropped by Everton due to 'breach of club discipline'

title: George Michael's Faith guitar sells for £180k after auction row
description: Image source, Michael Putland/Getty ImagesByKatie RazzallCulture and media editor and Helen BushbyCulture reporterUpdated 5 hours agoThe guitar George
body: Image source, Michael Putland/Getty ImagesByKatie RazzallCulture and media editor and Helen BushbyCulture reporterUpdated 5 hours agoThe guitar George Michael performed with in his 1987 Faith music video has sold for £180,000 at auction, after a row over the sale of memorabilia related to the singer.The guitar was one of more than 30 items auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant. The sale fetched a total of £238,000 excluding buyers' premium.Bailey died in 2014 and the items were sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Belcher declined to comment.Sworders chairman Guy Schooling said Belcher had been "nothing but delightful" during their interactions over the past two-and-a-half years."There are two ways of looking at this - it can be cashing in, or it can be a bit of a memorial and a tribute to Siobhan, and that's the way we've looked at it," he told BBC News.The auction house billed the 32 lots, including signed photographs, invitations to events and presentation CDs and discs, as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".'Dishonourable and shameful'Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will. Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.There is no suggestion that Belcher did not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin. In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considered the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name was "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" was "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".Bailey asked that the auction should not go ahead, or be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.Image source, Pete Still/Redferns via Getty ImagesImage caption, The memorabilia on sale includes signed photographs of Wham! and George Michael on stageSiobhan Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories."I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said."She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."The guitar was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".The auction's biggest sales£180,000 - The Rockabilly Rebel guitar from the Faith video, with original hardshell case and leather guitar strap £7,000 - A Queen Five Live EP sleeve signed by Brian May, John Deacon, Roger Taylor, George Michael and Lisa Stansfield£5,000 - A Faith Tour ringbound itinerary from George Michael's 1988 world tour£4,800 - A presentation CD of George Michael's Older £4,500 - A gold disc of Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go£4,200 - A gold disc of George Michael's I Want Your SexOther items on sale included a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Andrew Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party."I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.Speaking before Thursday's auction, he said "she would never have consented" to it, adding that the sale "breaks my heart"."I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax [tour itinerary] and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".Bailey acknowledged that Belcher had a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.George Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: George Michael's Faith guitar sells for £180k after auction row

title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
description: Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.The prime minister called
body: Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected."This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case."We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse. It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off. Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores.Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.Bally Auluk, a national officer at the Usdaw shopworkers union, said this week had been "incredibly distressing" for Poundland staff.He claimed staff were having to "watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1".He said Williams had "reluctantly" kicked off the administration process, to give the business time to find a rescue deal, adding that Usdaw was urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider.There is also a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable"."As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business."I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.

schema.headline: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse

title: Spain Urda train crash: Shock of tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
description: The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at
body: The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls."You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60. He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital."There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine."One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.

schema.headline: Spain Urda train crash: Shock of tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
description: People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards gr
body: People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said."This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice."The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.There would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament, Miller added."Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said."Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" or the buffer that the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

schema.headline: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall

title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentChancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spo
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentChancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.How much is being spent on welfare?The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise, external from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.The problem of NeetsWhat could cutting the benefits bill mean?Looming reports may offer optionsThe final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25, external, so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access, external, although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more, external to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits, suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.Graphics by Rob England

schema.headline: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?

title: Jacksepticeye: YouTuber talks Hitman, Bloodborne and new projects
description: 'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out Image source, IO InteractiveImage caption, Seán McLoughlin, aka Jacksept
body: 'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out Image source, IO InteractiveImage caption, Seán McLoughlin, aka Jacksepticeye, has been taking on more voice acting rolesByAndrew Rogers and Tom RichardsonBBC NewsbeatThe world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.Image source, IO InteractiveImage caption, McLoughlin plays influencer Finnvictus in the latest Hitman missionMcLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him. He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans."If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin. "If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it."This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.Image source, PlayStationImage caption, Bloodborne, originally released on PlayStation 4, is considered an all-time classicEarlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials. McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it. He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly."If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says."They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about."I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says."So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."'Rise of anti-communities'Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely"."Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says."But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."Image source, AdHoc StudioImage caption, McLoughlin also appeared as reformed villain Punch Up in superhero adventure game DispatchPhysical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate  discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released"."I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says."It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything. "But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries."Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says."So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days. "It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation."I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes. "I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says."Because I think there's too much of that in the world." Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Jacksepticeye: YouTuber talks Hitman, Bloodborne and new projects
